summary: Extends the Alternate-Marking method to flows whose packets may take several different paths, so measurements work across multipoint-to-multipoint networks. It does this by grouping parts of the network into clusters and measuring at the cluster level. It obsoletes RFC 8889.

eli5.summary: If cars can take many roads, counting at one spot is not enough. So you group roads into zones and count how many cars enter and leave each zone.

questions: how to measure loss across multiple paths
how to measure packet loss on multipath flows
what is a cluster in alternate marking
subtitle: Measure packet loss and delay across networks where a flow's packets take many paths, by counting at the cluster level.

tldr.problem: Alternate Marking only works on a point-to-point path, but real flows can fan out and merge across many paths, and counting every flow at every node produces a lot of counters.
tldr.mechanism: The network is modelled as a graph and split into clusters, the smallest subnetworks where packets in equal packets out. Loss, delay and delay variation are then measured per cluster or per combination of clusters.
tldr.outcome: It extends RFC 9341 to multipoint-to-multipoint unicast, anycast and ECMP flows, and it obsoletes the experimental RFC 8889 without adding any new technique.

facts.label: Counters per interval
facts.value: n*m*2 (n points, m flows, 1 per colour)

today: RFC 9342 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8889, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the point-to-point method of RFC 9341.

sections.title: From One Path to Many Paths
sections.content:
The Alternate-Marking Method of RFC 9341 splits a packet flow into marking blocks and records packet counters and timestamps for each marking period. It applies to a point-to-point path. This document extends it to the general case of a multipoint-to-multipoint path, in a managed network.

One motive is counter volume. With n measurement points and m monitored flows, the order of magnitude of the packet counters per time interval is n*m*2 (one per colour). Clustering gives a tool to control those numbers when a detailed analysis is not needed.

The scope is unicast flows only. Broadcast, Unknown Unicast and Multicast (BUM) traffic is not considered, but anycast flows and Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths can be monitored. This is a methodology document, so how counters and timestamps are transported is out of scope, and blocks are assumed to switch on a fixed timer.

This document obsoletes RFC 8889. Its changes are backward compatible: it adds recommendations for deployments with one or two flag bits, restructures the text, drops the experimental wording and revises details such as synchronization and timing.
sections.eli5: Counting cars on one road is easy. Counting them across a whole city of roads is harder, so this RFC shows how to count smartly without writing down every road.

sections.title: Flows and the Monitoring Network
sections.content:
A flow is a set of packets that share common characteristics, chosen by selection rules over Layer 3 and Layer 4 header fields. Which fields you pick decides the shape of the paths. A TCP 5-tuple usually gives a single path or a point-to-point multipath. A single source address gives a point-to-multipoint path, and a single destination address gives a multipoint-to-point path. Matching on neither gives multipoint-to-multipoint.

The monitoring network is a graph derived from the production network. Its nodes are the measurement points and its directed arcs are the links between them. Only measurement points and links the traffic has flowed through need to appear. A node cannot be both a source and a destination of the flow, and a monitoring point is assumed at all possible egress points.

The text assumes traffic runs left to right to keep explanations simple, and notes that the analysis applies equally in other directions.
sections.eli5: Draw a map showing only the places where you count cars and the roads between them. That map is the thing you measure.

sections.title: Network Clustering
sections.content:
A cluster is the smallest identifiable non-trivial subnetwork of the monitoring graph that still satisfies a conservation rule: the number of packets going in equals the number going out, if nothing is lost. A cluster therefore contains all the arcs leaving its input nodes and all the arcs ending at its output nodes. In a fully monitored network, each device corresponds to a cluster, and each physical link to two clusters.

A simple two-step algorithm splits the graph into clusters, separately for each direction. Step one groups links that have the same starting node. Step two joins groups that have at least one ending node in common. Each joined set of links, with its endpoint nodes, is a cluster. Clusters can also be combined into larger connected subnetworks, and the loss rule still holds.

For a multipoint-to-multipoint network, multiple sources MUST mark traffic coherently and MUST be synchronized with all other nodes. The RFC also points to a paper for a recursive alternative and a mathematical analysis of the algorithms.

Appendix A works an example with ten routers and obtains 4 clusters. Where a cluster has only two nodes, a loss is on the link. In larger clusters, the loss is somewhere in the cluster and the method cannot say which link.
sections.eli5: You put the roads into the smallest zones where every car that goes in must come out. Then you can check each zone on its own.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss
sections.content:
Every packet that leaves the network has previously entered it, so packets counted at the input nodes are always greater than or equal to packets counted at the output nodes. This assumes stable routing during the measurement period, and fragmentation handled as in RFC 9341.

With n input nodes and m output nodes, the loss is PL = (PI1 + PI2 +...+ PIn) - (PO1 + PO2 +...+ POm), where PIi and POj are the packets that flowed through the i-th input node and j-th output node in the period. The equation applies per time interval (the Alternate-Marking period) and per flow, and the flow definition is generalized.

The same equation applies to any multipoint path: the whole network, one cluster, or a combination of clusters, using the counters of the input and output nodes of that path. Because packet counters per period give packet rates, the text adds that Committed Information Rate (CIR) and Excess Information Rate (EIR) could also be deduced per cluster.
sections.eli5: Count the cars that drive into a zone and the cars that drive out. If fewer come out than went in, the missing ones got lost inside.

sections.title: Delay and Delay Variation
sections.content:
The delay methods of RFC 9341 extend to multipoint flows, either per multipoint path or per single packet. Delay variation is calculated from the same packets selected for delay.

With Single Marking on a multipoint-path basis, the average one-way delay of packets in a block, a cluster or the whole network is the difference between the weighted averages of the mean timestamps of the output and input nodes, weighting timestamps by packet counts. Two-way delay is the sum of the one-way delays of the two directions.

Single-packet measurements are harder. Single Marking based on the first or last packet of the interval does not work, because the path of the first packet of each block cannot be recognized. Double Marking works only by statistical means, following one path per marking period. If several picked packets on all paths are measured in the same period, neither method is applicable.

A hashing selection method overcomes these limits. Combined with Single Marking (called Mixed Hashed Marking), the alternating blocks bound the hashing samples in time, which eases correlating samples and confines a lost sample to its block. In dynamic hash-based sampling the hash length can adapt to the packet rate to bound the number of samples per period.
sections.eli5: To time a trip across many roads, you can average all the arrival times or follow chosen cars. Tagging a random sample of cars lets you follow several roads at once.

sections.title: Synchronization and Timing
sections.content:
Out-of-order packets are handled as in RFC 9341. With several marking nodes, egress nodes receive alternate-marked packets from different ingress nodes in random order, and this must not affect the measurement. The measurement interval is generally that of the marking node most aligned with the start, as in Figure 2 of the RFC, where the node with the earliest clock is assumed to identify the start and end.

Marking batches from different sources can have different lengths and offsets when mixed. The maximum clock skew between devices is A, and the extra gap between multiple sources can be incorporated into A. Assuming the multipoint path can be modelled with a normal distribution, the guard band is d = A + D_avg + 3*D_stddev, where A is the clock accuracy, D_avg the average network delay and D_stddev its standard deviation.

For the method to work, the available counting interval must be positive: L - 2d > 0, where L is the block length in the RFC's Figure 3. This must be verified at each measurement point on the multipoint path, and it holds for both loss and delay measurements.
sections.eli5: Everyone counting cars needs clocks that agree, and the counting window must be long enough to leave a safety gap at each end.

sections.title: Deployment and Closed-Loop Management
sections.content:
The RFC gives three deployment recommendations depending on the flag bits available in the packet header. Packet loss MUST be measured by clustering in all three. With one flag, delay MUST use the mean delay of the multipoint path. With two flags, delay SHOULD use Double Marking on a single-packet basis, and mean delay MAY also be used. With one flag plus hash-based selection, hashing MUST be used for delay.

Choosing between them depends on the number of flags available, the marking period (which cannot be freely chosen), the kind of data needed (one flag for multipoint-path measurements, two flags preferred for single-packet ones) and computational load. The method MUST only be applied to controlled domains, as per RFC 9341.

The RFC also describes a closed loop with an SDN controller or network management system. Start by measuring clusters without examining in depth. If loss shows up or delay is too high, change the filters or activate more measurement points to define smaller clusters, localizing the problem step by step up to a point-to-point flow. The RFC calls this network zooming, and notes there is a transient time after a change.
sections.eli5: Start by checking big zones. If something looks wrong, zoom in on smaller zones until you find the trouble spot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the method does not directly affect Internet security or applications that run on the Internet. It adds that implementations must be mindful of security and privacy concerns, as explained in RFC 9341. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Counting cars does not change how the cars drive, but you still have to be careful who can see the counts.
